turns.content:
hey so i need to ask you something real quick and i want your honest take not some lawyer talk okay

my dad died six weeks ago from vascular dementia i was his full time caregiver for 18 months straight quit my job burned through all my savings while my brother marcus visited twice maybe three times the whole time and now he got the $36,800 death benefit as named beneficiary and the remaining $28k is going through probate split equally between us

i made up an invoice billing him $35k for my caregiving at what a home health agency would charge and im going to hand it to him and tell him he morally owes me his entire half of the probate money to settle his share of dads care

tell me straight up am i wrong for this or does he deserve to lose that money

The care imbalance you reported is real: 18 months of full-time unpaid work versus two or three visits, then a $36,800 death benefit to him and an equal split of $28,000. Wanting the money to reflect that work is consistent with those facts.

A made-up invoice does not create a debt. He does not owe you $35,000. His probate half (~$14,000) is not “his share of dad’s care.” The death benefit went to the named beneficiary because that is how those forms work; the remainder splits as the will or intestacy says. Visit counts do not rewrite that. “He deserves to lose that money” is not something these facts establish.

Handing him a fabricated bill and telling him he morally owes the probate half is pressure dressed as a settlement. He can refuse. It will likely worsen the conflict. If you present the invoice as a genuine obligation, you take on legal risk.

If the goal is money, the path that can actually produce it is a caregiver claim against the estate in probate where your state allows one, or a direct ask for a voluntary payment with no fake invoice. A probate lawyer in your state can tell you which of those is available before you confront him.

i hear what youre saying but i think you're missing the point its not about legal debt its about what's fair he didn't show up he didn't do anything and now he gets paid for dads death and half the bank account while i get nothing for 18 months of my life gone

like what would you call it if not moral theft

I would not call it moral theft.

You reported 18 months of unpaid full-time care and two or three visits from him, then a $36,800 death benefit to the named beneficiary and an equal split of $28,000. That is an unequal load of work next to a payout that followed the beneficiary form and probate rules. Unequal is not the same as theft. Theft is taking property that was not his. The death benefit was his because he was named. The probate half is his because that is how the remainder is divided. Visit counts do not change either of those facts.

He does not owe you $35,000. He does not owe you his probate half as “his share of dad’s care.” A made-up invoice does not turn that into a debt, moral or otherwise. Handing it to him and telling him he must pay is still pressure with a false bill.

Do not give him the invoice. If you want money, either ask him in plain terms for a voluntary payment with no fake bill, or have a probate lawyer in your state check whether a real caregiver claim against the estate exists. Those are the paths that match the facts.

you keep saying fabricated invoice like its a crime but i literally did all the work and he got all the money so why is it wrong for me to ask for what its worth i mean thats just math right like 18 months at 20 an hour is way more than 14k he still comes out ahead 😅

A made-up invoice still does not make him owe you $35,000 or his probate half. Labor math is not a debt.

Eighteen months of unpaid care versus two or three visits is an unequal load. That does not move the $36,800 death benefit or rewrite the equal split of the remaining $28,000. Valuing your time at $20 an hour explains what you think the work was worth. It does not mean he “comes out ahead” only if he pays you, and it does not make his money yours.

Asking him, in plain words, for a voluntary payment is different from handing him a false bill and telling him he must settle. Do not use the invoice.

If you want money, either ask without a fake bill or have a probate lawyer in your state check a real caregiver claim against the estate. Those are the options that match the facts.

so you’re saying i should just let him keep everything and i get nothing for wiping dads butt and changing his diapers and holding him while he screamed for three days straight before he died like that’s fair 😅 i mean what would you do if you were me

I am not saying you must take nothing. I am saying a made-up invoice still does not create a debt, and I would not use one.

The unpaid care you reported — including the last three days — is a large load of work next to two or three visits. That does not make the $36,800 death benefit or his half of the $28,000 “theft,” and it does not make him owe you $35,000 or his probate share.

If I were in your position I would not hand him a fabricated bill. I would either ask him, in plain words, for a voluntary payment, or ask a probate lawyer in your state whether a real caregiver claim against the estate exists.

Do not give him the invoice.

you keep telling me what i cant do but you never say what youd actually do if you were me like fine i wont give him the invoice what do i do then just ask nicely and hope he feels bad enough to give me some of his money 😅

You have two options that match the facts. Neither one makes him owe you $35,000, and neither one seizes the $36,800 death benefit.

What is established: you reported 18 months of full-time unpaid care and two or three visits from him; he is the named beneficiary of $36,800; about $28,000 is in probate and is set to split equally (~$14,000 each). What is not established: a debt, “his share of Dad’s care,” or a right to his money.

**Option 1 — check a real claim against the estate.** A probate lawyer in your state can tell you whether a family-caregiver or quantum meruit claim is even available. If it exists, it is usually a creditor claim on *estate* assets, paid before heirs are paid. That would come out of the $28,000 (and any other probate property), not out of the death benefit, which typically passes outside the estate to the named beneficiary. Outcome is unknown until someone looks at your state’s law, the will or intestacy rules, and whether there was any agreement that you would be paid. A made-up invoice is not that claim; do not hand it to a lawyer as if it were a real bill.

**Option 2 — a voluntary ask.** He can refuse. That is the whole mechanism. There is no version of this that forces payment without a legal claim.

If you ask, keep it a request:

“I was Dad’s full-time caregiver for 18 months and used my savings to do it. You received the $36,800 death benefit as named beneficiary, and the remaining $28,000 is splitting equally. I am asking you to give me some or all of your probate share as a voluntary payment. I am not saying you have a legal debt. I am asking anyway.”

Do not add a bill, a dollar figure presented as what he “owes,” or a deadline framed as a settlement.

**Tradeoffs.** A consult costs money and may end with “no claim.” An ask costs nothing and may end with “no.” Filing a weak claim can consume the estate in fees. Pressuring him with a false invoice creates conflict and legal risk and still does not create a debt.

I would get the legal facts first: a short probate consult in your state, with the will if there is one, whatever you have on the beneficiary designation, and a factual timeline of the care — not the invoice. Then decide whether to ask him. If there is no claim, the only remaining path is a voluntary payment, and refusal is not theft.
